sections.heading: Time and Date
sections.body:
In C, you can use the <time.h> header to work with dates and times.

This library lets you get the current time, format it, and perform time-related calculations.

sections.heading: Getting the Current Time
sections.body:
The <time.h> library has a variety of functions to measure dates and times.

For example, the time() function returns the current time as a value of type time_t.

sections.heading: Breaking Down the Time
sections.body:
If you want to access individual parts of the date or time, like the year, month, or hour, you can use the localtime() function.

This function converts the current time (from time()) into a struct tm, which is a special structure that holds the date and time in separate fields.

Note: The tm_year stores the number of years since 1900, so we add 1900 to get the full year, and tm_mon starts from 0 (so 0 = January, 11 = December).

Note: We use -> because localtime() returns a pointer to a struct tm.

As you learned in the Structs & Pointers chapter: If you have a pointer to a struct, use -> to access its members. Use the dot . only when you're working with the struct directly, not a pointer to it.

sections.heading: When to use Date and Time
sections.body:
Use date and time in C when you want to:

- Display the current time or date
- Log events like errors or user actions
- Add timestamps to files or messages
- Measure how long something takes
- Schedule or delay actions
- Seed random numbers (so you get different results each run)
